# What to Optimize

Agent harness optimization changes the execution system around a fixed target model. The first decisions are **what may change, what remains fixed, and who judges improvement**.

## What to Hold Fixed and What to Change

| Role | Examples | May the Optimizer Change It? |
|---|---|---|
| Target model | Large language model (LLM) weights, decoding policy | Fixed in principle. Treat any change as a separate version |
| Harness | Prompts, context, tool wrappers and tool policy, workflow, memory, recovery | Yes, but define the scope in advance |
| Environment | Browser, database, compiler, simulator | Fixed in principle |
| Evaluator | Score, cost, safety measurement | No. Keep it outside the optimizer |

For example, if tools are called in a poor order, the workflow can be changed. In contrast, changing how the evaluator assigns scores to make a candidate appear better is not allowed.

The evaluator measures outcomes but does not decide whether to accept a change. The acceptance rule $V$ accepts or rejects a candidate according to predefined conditions. The optimizer $O$, which produces candidates, cannot change the evaluator or $V$.

@fig-optimization-boundary shows this boundary. An execution result is used to produce a candidate $H'_t$, and only a candidate that passes external evaluation is saved as the next version $H_{t+1}$.

![An editable harness around a fixed target model, with the evaluator and acceptance rule separated from the optimizer. An execution result produces a candidate, and only a candidate that passes external evaluation is saved.](images/optimization-boundary.svg){#fig-optimization-boundary fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Mathematical Formulation

A task $x$, target agent $A_{\theta,H}$, and environment $E$ produce one trajectory $\tau$.

$$
\tau \sim P(\tau \mid x, A_{\theta,H}, E)
$$

Define the evaluation value of harness $H$ over task distribution $\mathcal{D}$ as

$$
J_{\mathcal{D}}(H)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},\,\tau}[s(\tau)]
$$

This is the average score $s(\tau)$ across different tasks. Harness optimization keeps the target model parameters $\theta$ fixed while updating $H_t$ to $H_{t+1}$ to improve this value.

## Separate One Execution from Updates for Future Runs

A single execution solves the current task. Harness optimization uses the execution record as evidence to change the harness and saves the change for use on subsequent tasks.

If the two are conflated, methods that only increase thinking time within one response would count as harness improvements. A change must persist to future executions.

## Included and Excluded Changes

| Change | Treatment in This Book |
|---|---|
| Add ordinary execution records to memory | Merely a state update; not called optimization by itself |
| Use failures to change memory content or the read/write policy, then save the change after external evaluation | Included in harness optimization |
| Increase the number of samples or reflection rounds for one task | Test-time scaling; excluded unless the change persists to the next run |
| Update the compute allocation policy from execution results and save it for future use | Included in harness optimization |
| Change target model weights $\theta$ through fine-tuning or reinforcement learning (RL) | Target model optimization; separate from harness optimization |

Reflexion stores reflections after failures in memory and uses them in subsequent trials [@shinn2023reflexion]. This is an example of persistence across trials within the same task, not an evaluation of an artifact promoted across independent future tasks. Separate external evaluation is needed to determine whether the change improves performance in general.

Harness-R1 keeps the target model fixed and uses a separate editor to generate a candidate $H'_t$. The editor is trained, but the harness is the final object being updated [@shao2026harnessr1].

## Five Decisions Before an Experiment

- **Edit scope:** Files, hooks, prompts, and tool schemas that may change
- **Fixed conditions:** APIs, permissions, timeouts, and output schemas
- **Persisted state:** What remains across tasks
- **Evaluation metrics:** How to aggregate quality, cost, latency, and failure rate
- **Acceptance rule:** Conditions for accepting or rejecting a candidate and rolling back if needed

The boundary should be explicit enough to state, for example, that "the pre-action hook may change, but the evaluator and tool permissions may not." Without fixing the boundary first, the source of an improvement cannot be reproduced.

## Key Points

Harness optimization keeps the target model and environment fixed in principle and changes only the harness within the permitted scope. It separates candidate generation from external evaluation and carries accepted changes forward to future tasks.
